why: Library lessons no longer carry grammar tips (their explanations moved to the grammar unit 'First phrases'), and 'What does X mean?' questions were cut where a typed answer covers the same phrase. Kept here for reuse, e.g. as review items or notes.

tips.title: Two Worlds: Formal and Informal
tips.explanation: Every Italian interaction splits into formal or informal. Use 'ciao' with friends and family. Use 'buongiorno' or 'buonasera' with strangers, elders, or anyone you'd call 'Sir' or 'Ma'am'. Getting this right matters — Italians notice immediately.

tips.title: Greeting by the Clock
tips.explanation: 'Buongiorno' covers morning through early afternoon. 'Buonasera' takes over from late afternoon onward. But 'buonanotte' is NOT a greeting — it's only for bedtime, like saying 'sleep well'. You would never walk into a restaurant at 9 PM and say 'buonanotte'.

tips.title: Salve — Your Safety Net
tips.explanation: Not sure if someone is a 'ciao' person or a 'buongiorno' person? Say 'salve'. It works at any time, in any register — perfectly neutral. From Latin, meaning 'be well'.

tips.title: Scusi vs. Scusa — The Formal/Informal Split Again
tips.explanation: Just like 'ciao' vs 'buongiorno', Italian splits 'excuse me' into formal and informal. 'Scusi' for strangers and formal situations. 'Scusa' for friends. When in doubt, use 'scusi' — being too polite is never a problem.

tips.title: Permesso — A Word English Doesn't Have
tips.explanation: 'Permesso' is said when you physically need to pass through or enter someone's space. On a crowded bus, pushing through a doorway, entering someone's home — say 'permesso'. It's like 'coming through' but polite. There's no exact English equivalent.

tips.title: Prego Does Everything
tips.explanation: 'Prego' is the reply to 'grazie' (you're welcome), but Italians use it for much more. A waiter hands you the menu: 'Prego.' Someone asks if they can sit: 'Prego!' (Please, go ahead.) It's Italian for 'help yourself'.

tips.title: Stai vs. Sta — Informal and Formal Again
tips.explanation: 'Come stai?' is informal (friends). 'Come sta?' is formal (strangers, elders). Same split as 'ciao' vs 'buongiorno' and 'scusa' vs 'scusi'. This pattern runs through ALL of Italian — get used to it!

example.english: Good morning, professor. How are you?

tips.title: Stare, Not Essere
tips.explanation: To say how you feel, Italian uses 'stare' — NOT 'essere'. 'Sto bene' (I'm well) is correct. 'Sono bene' is WRONG. For now just memorize 'sto bene' and 'sto male' as chunks — the full verb comes later.

tips.title: Always Ask Back
tips.explanation: In Italian, answering 'How are you?' without asking back is rude. Always add 'e tu?' (informal) or 'e Lei?' (formal). The full pattern: Bene, grazie, e tu? (Well, thanks, and you?)

tips.title: Your Two Lifelines
tips.explanation: When a conversation moves too fast, you have two essential tools: 'Non capisco' (I don't understand) to signal the problem, and 'Può ripetere?' (Can you repeat?) to ask for help. Use them freely — Italians appreciate the effort more than they judge the struggle.

tips.title: Come si dice...? — Learn Mid-Conversation
tips.explanation: 'Come si dice...?' means 'How do you say...?' It lets you learn new words right inside a conversation. Point at something and ask 'Come si dice questo in italiano?' (How do you say this in Italian?) — and you'll get a mini lesson on the spot.

tips.title: Va bene vs. D'accordo
tips.explanation: Both mean 'okay', but they feel different. 'Va bene' is relaxed — 'alright, fine'. 'D'accordo' emphasizes agreement — 'agreed, deal'. You'll hear 'va bene' more in casual conversation and 'd'accordo' when confirming plans.

tips.title: Buon + Event
tips.explanation: Italians wish each other well constantly. The pattern is 'buon/buona/buoni/buone' (good) + the occasion: 'Buon compleanno!' (Happy birthday!), 'Buon viaggio!' (Have a good trip!), 'Buone vacanze!' (Happy holidays!).

tips.title: Auguri & Complimenti
tips.explanation: 'Auguri!' is a one-word 'best wishes!' for any occasion. 'Complimenti!' = well done / congratulations. 'Congratulazioni!' is more formal — used for big achievements (marriage, graduation).

tips.title: Daily Wishes
tips.explanation: 'Buona giornata!' (Have a good day!), 'Buona serata!' (Have a good evening!), 'Buon appetito!' (Enjoy your meal!) — these are said constantly. Italians never just say 'bye' without one of these.
